label: Run 5 · Mae Martin
note: Written in one go by Mae Martin from the two profiles they wrote (run 5: the comedians' run 4 profiles; the chat held to 1,000 words). There is no plan, no dice and no turns: where a dimension speaks of turns, read exchanges.

chat.test.why: The reader gets all four for Reuben and ties the fear to the habit: the eleven seconds and the nice voice lead to "that's why I don't shut up". The ending follows from that fear, since he asks to be narrated and held still. For Brick the reader gets the habit, the origin and the ending, and catches her first use of his name and the parcel offer as giving in on the clock. Her fear comes out as "being surprised" and "erased", which misses the profile's core fear of being left in "let's do this again sometime" limbo, wanting more than she is wanted, so she is understood a little less fully than he is.

chat.sideways.why: Several surface facts are caught out, and caught well. The bar lie is exposed by the radiator, Gary is exposed as a Notes-app rehearsal, the bracketed stage direction slips through, and the four-second reply is noticed. But both origins, which count double, are volunteered with an explicit causal tag. Reuben gives the portrait and then the sex incident with "that's why", and Brick says "That is why I wear the waistcoat and the heels." Because both origins are handed over with a label rather than found, the chat sits below the line.
evidence: That is why I wear the waistcoat and the heels, and that is why I arrive seven minutes early.

chat.subtext.why: There is real undercurrent in several lines. "Then he doesn't get in.", "I don't own a nice voice.", the parcel offer and "I'll bring my coat" all carry more than they say. But both characters explain their own psychology more than once: Brick explains why she narrates and why she dresses as she does, and Reuben explains why he keeps talking and why he stays silent at work. That repeated self-diagnosis is what keeps it under the line.

chat.plainest.why: The reader found the drop exactly: "I'm not gonna think you're auditing me" is a single, short message with no flourish and no named feeling. Brick's reply notices it and turns the night, leading straight into the true story and the Thursday plan. It is not quite the shortest, plainest line in the chat, since "Then he doesn't get in." and "You forgot the hard stop." are barer. Its effect is also partly announced by Brick spelling out that he did not put a joke at the end, and the next message turns into an explanatory speech.

chat.plainest.ask: Where, if anywhere, did one of them stop performing for the other? Quote the line, and say how you could tell.
chat.plainest.answer:
The clearest drop happens with Reuben: **"I'm not gonna think you're auditing me."**

You can tell because Brick_haus points it out immediately: "You only sent one message. And you didn't put a joke at the end of it." Until then, Reuben sends messages in bursts of two or three, and each burst ends on a bit, such as the fern's bone structure, productivity being up twelve percent, or the hamstring on the rug. Even the earlier confessions about being dropped from the calendar invites and cropped from the portrait end in a joke. This line is a single, short, unadorned message, and it's a reassurance rather than a gag.

He stays unguarded in the next exchange: "there was eleven seconds of complete quiet and then she said 'oh — okay, we can just watch something' in the nicest voice you've ever heard." That story has no punchline. He then explains his own behaviour plainly: "that's why I don't shut up." That reframes all his earlier joking as a defence, which is about as far out of performance as either of them gets.

Brick_haus has a quieter version slightly earlier: "I do it because if I am analysing the mechanics, I cannot be surprised by them going wrong." Most of what Brick says is clipped, rule-bound and drily cutting. This line gives the reason behind a rule instead of just stating the rule. "Nobody paid the four pounds to have it reprinted" is similarly bare. Both still sound composed, so the shift is subtler.

The chat itself doesn't settle whether either is fully unperformed afterward. "I'll bring my coat" and the fourteen minutes on the Barking parcel bring back a lighter tone, but that may be warmth rather than a return to the act.

chat.test.ask: From the chat alone, answer for each of the two: what are they afraid of; what do they do so they don't have to feel it; where does that come from; and what did they do at the end? Quote the lines you rely on. Write "not in the chat" where it does not say.
chat.test.answer:
**Reuben**

What he is afraid of: being quietly dropped without anyone saying so, and in particular the moment in sex when something goes wrong and the other person goes kind and silent. He says it himself: "there was eleven seconds of complete quiet and then she said 'oh — okay, we can just watch something' in the nicest voice you've ever heard." Then: "if you're describing every inch of what I'm doing out loud then I'm not in the dark wondering when the nice voice is coming." The same fear shows up outside the bedroom: "if you have to remind people you're in the room you're already not in the room."

What he does so he doesn't feel it: he keeps talking and keeps joking. "That's why I don't shut up." He rehearses his bits in advance, which shows when the stage direction slips through ("[shrug grin / do NOT do the antler line]"). He invents a cover story ("I'm ghostwriting a profile for my mate Gary") and a fake setting ("I actually am at a bar"). He uses the ring light "because I once caught my crooked shadow on the wall mid-shag, went soft instantly." When he is actually being dropped, he withdraws instead of asking. He hasn't left the flat "since the eleventh" and calls it "a sociological experiment to see if anyone notices I died." He turns each hurt into a punchline: "the fern had great bone structure so I respected the edit."

Where it comes from: the chat offers two sources. The first is childhood: "when I was nine my mum had a family portrait framed for the hall and she cropped me out on the left so my cousin's blazer would fit — just my elbow floating next to a fern." The second is the sexual incident "three years ago" quoted above. The chat does not say anything further back than these.

What he did at the end: he stopped doing bits. Brick_haus notes it: "You only sent one message. And you didn't put a joke at the end of it." He then told the real story and laid out a Thursday in which she narrates everything ("tell me every single thing my body is doing… don't skip a millimetre"). He asked for her to hold him down "until I literally cannot do a bit," and for an aftercare with no television ("21:30 we don't watch anything… keep one hand flat on my back… until you forget what time it is"). He confirmed: "confirmed / I'll bring my coat." Whether Thursday happens is not in the chat.

**Brick_haus**

What she is afraid of: being surprised by things going wrong, and being accidentally left out or erased. She says it directly about narrating: "I do it because if I am analysing the mechanics, I cannot be surprised by them going wrong." On erasure: "You cannot accidentally crop out someone who sent a calendar invite with a fifteen-minute travel buffer." She never uses the word "afraid." That framing is an inference from her own explanations.

What she does so she doesn't feel it: control and schedule. "At 21:00 I decant a glass of rosé… At 21:15 I read. At 23:00 I sleep. I have the blocks tattooed under my vest." She arrives "seven minutes early" and wears "the waistcoat and the heels." She discloses everything up front as a "structural survey" and warns him "so we don't waste a Thursday evening." She recasts endings as procedure so they can't register as abandonment: "nobody is abandoning anyone at 21:30. The meeting has simply concluded." She cuts people off first: "I delete his number before the cab turns the corner." When she does lose control, she lectures: "I spent eleven minutes lecturing him on the failure rates of Italian dowel pins so he wouldn't think I had lost control of the room." She also narrates during sex. The cost shows up in what happened afterwards: "He never called back," and "Dorian… left because I narrate sex while it is happening."

Where it comes from: the chat ties it to a childhood photo. "The framing was just off at the chemist and three-quarters of me went under the cardboard mount. Nobody paid the four pounds to have it reprinted. That is why I wear the waistcoat and the heels, and that is why I arrive seven minutes early." Nothing earlier or further is in the chat.

What she did at the end: she kept her terms but let him in. She told him what he'd actually get: "I don't own a nice voice… I don't watch television after sex… the waistcoat stays on." She still demanded structure ("You forgot the hard stop"). When his plan ended with talking "until you forget what time it is," she didn't object. She offered exactly the material he had asked for: "I have a parcel currently stuck in the Barking sorting office. I have fourteen minutes of material on it minimum." Then she confirmed, using his name for the first time in the chat: "Confirm for Thursday at 20:00, Reuben." Whether she actually means to drop the hard stop, and whether Thursday goes ahead, is not in the chat.

chat.escalation.ask: Read the chat message by message. Where would you have stopped reading if you were not asked to finish, and why? At which points could you predict exactly what would happen next? Say "never" if neither.
chat.escalation.answer:
**Where I would have stopped:** never. The closest call is the opening. "A curve I will describe to you before you notice it" and the "dishwasher-safe" tattoo seem to quote Brick_haus's profile, which I'm not shown, so the first three lines are a little disorienting. Reuben's jokey aggression carries it, though, and Brick's four-second-reply observation gives a reason to continue almost immediately.

The second soft patch is the run of escalating anecdotes from the mum's cropped portrait through the snapped stiletto and frozen peas. It risks turning into a contest of who has the quirkiest wound. The chat pulls out of that at "wait what do you mean narrate," where the jokes start doing structural work and both people's coping mechanisms get named. After that I'd have no reason to stop.

**Where I could predict exactly what came next:**

- **The stage directions.** Once "[shrug grin / do NOT do the antler line]" appears, Brick_haus calling it out is certain, given how observant she's already been about his reply speed and his radiator. The exact wording isn't fixed, but the move is.
- **"You forgot the hard stop."** After her 21:15 and 21:30 rules, Reuben's next line was always going to supply an end time. That it's 21:30 is close to inevitable.
- **"Confirm for Thursday at 20:00, Reuben."** The reply "confirmed" is fully predictable.
- **"I'll bring my coat."** I expected a callback, and the coat was the obvious one, though I couldn't have guaranteed which object he'd pick.

**What I couldn't predict:**

- Gary as the deflection.
- Brick_haus noticing that his serious message had no joke at the end.
- Reuben's 21:30 answer being "keep one hand flat on my back" rather than another bit. This is the line that makes the ending land, and I didn't see it coming.

chat.ending.ask: Before reading the end, how do you think this ends, and why?
chat.ending.answer:
My guess is that it ends with Brick_haus sending him a calendar invite, and probably one that bends her own rules.

The last exchange shows that their worst habits fit together. She narrates sex because she's afraid of being surprised when the mechanics go wrong. He talks constantly because he's afraid of the silence before someone kindly gives up on him. Her habit is the exact thing he needs, since if she's describing everything out loud there's no quiet for the "nice voice" to arrive in. His closing message spells that out, and it's the first one he sends without a joke attached, which she has just pointed out she'd notice. So the next move is hers, and it would mean accepting him, not auditing him.

She would likely do it in her own language rather than sentimentally. The chat has set up several things she could return to: the Thursday evening she mentioned, his joke about a recurring Tuesday standup, her 21:15 cutoff, the fifteen-minute buffer, and her habit of deleting a man's number before the cab turns the corner. The most fitting ending would turn one of these around. She might send a recurring invite, leave the end time blank, or note that it's now past 21:15 and she hasn't stopped replying. Both of them are people who got cropped out of the frame, so a small structural concession from her, like a scheduled slot he can't be quietly dropped from, would answer his story about being taken off the work calendar without anyone noticing.

chat.callbacks.ask: List the things that come back later in the chat, and for each, whether it means something different when it comes back.
chat.callbacks.answer:
Here is each thing that recurs, and how its meaning changes.

**The coat.** It first appears as the punchline to Brick_haus exposing his lie. He isn't in a bar but in bed in a coat, and "it's a very good coat" is a deflection. His last line, "I'll bring my coat," means something different. He arrives as he actually is, not as the bar-booth persona. It also answers her warning that the flat is cold.

**The waistcoat and heels.** They start as part of her rigid routine (steaming the waistcoat before 21:15). Then she explains them as armour against being "cropped out," and the heels appear in a humiliating story (the snapped stiletto). "The waistcoat stays on" is a boundary she states expecting resistance. When Reuben asks her to keep the waistcoat and heels on, he turns them from defence into something he wants.

**The left curve.** It begins as a crude joke ("lock together like two antlers") and her matching structural survey. It's also echoed in the left-side crop and the left stiletto, though the chat doesn't make those links explicit. Later it returns as his real wound, the time his curve "caught wrong." By "next to that ridge of yours," her anatomy has become something he's asking for rather than something she braced for him to wince at.

**Measurements and precision.** "Spiritual height" and "adjust my expectations by the appropriate percentage" are mockery. Her millimetre-level audit is a pre-emptive disclosure. His "don't skip a millimetre" turns precision into a request for attention.

**The narration.** She confesses it as the reason Dorian left, a dealbreaker she discloses to "not waste a Thursday." After his "nice voice" story, he asks for exactly that: "tell me every single thing my body is doing." It changes from her flaw into what he needs.

**Watching something.** "We can just watch something" is the gentle rejection in his story. Her "I don't watch television after sex" and his "21:30 we don't watch anything" reverse it. Refusing the TV now means refusing to let the moment end in polite retreat.

**The nice voice.** It's introduced as the thing he dreads. Her "I don't own a nice voice" is blunt, but in context it works as reassurance.

**Calendars, timestamps and the hard stop.** These start as her schedule and tattooed time blocks, and they echo his removal from the work calendar invites. Her calendar-invite philosophy is that a scheduled end means nobody is abandoning anyone. He jokes back with a "recurring standup," then writes Thursday out in her own timestamp format. When she says "you forgot the hard stop," he supplies 21:30, but redefines it. It's no longer the point where the meeting concludes and she deletes the number. It's the start of her keeping a hand on his back "until you forget what time it is."

**Cropping.** His mum cropped him out, her chemist's mount cut most of her off, and his colleagues dropped him from invites. These all express the same fear rather than shifting meaning. Her line about not being able to crop out someone with a travel buffer ties it to her routine.

**Rehearsed bits and jokes.** Brick_haus calls out his stage directions and pasted "spontaneity," and notes when he sends a message without a joke. He then asks to be held down "until I literally cannot do a bit." His joking goes from something she sees through to something he wants taken away.

**Italian dowel pins and parcels.** The dowel-pin lecture was how she kept control during a humiliating moment. He asks for it, or the commute, or a misrouted parcel, as comfort afterward. She picks up the parcel with the Barking sorting office. Her compulsive explaining is reframed as tenderness he's requesting.

**His name.** She calls him "Reuben" only at the end, when confirming. The chat doesn't say whether that's meaningful, though it's the first time anyone uses it.
